items.title: Pope says he leaves Peru with what he always admired
items.summary:
“I came to proclaim Christ to you, and I leave with the witness of the faith and devotion that I always admired in you,” Pope Leo said, as he said farewell to his second homeland after an intense 12-day journey through South America. The Holy Father’s plane took off around 2:30 p.m. local time, and he has a flight home of more than 14 hours. He’s set to arrive at Rome’s Fiumicino Airport on Tuesday, November 17, at 10:25 a.m. “I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family,” Pope Leo reflected. “It was here,” he said, “that you taught me how to be a Bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter.” 

Pope says he leaves Peru with what he always admired
items.t: Pope says he leaves Peru with what he always admired

items.title: Pope bids ‘hasta luego’ to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
items.summary:
LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.

Leo emerged from the Vatican’s residence in Lima to kick off his final morning, visiting a home for the elderly that he tended to during the COVID-19 pandemic, before a huge Mass at an air base in the Peruvian capital that’s expected to draw up to 1 million people.

Speaking to the crowd outside the residence, Leo thanked Peruvians for having accompanied him on his trip.

“Have a good day, thank you very much, and until later!” he said.

A trip and pontificate modeled on a missionary saint 

For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.

Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.

Mogrovejo, who lived from 1538-1606, is revered for having denounced abuses against Indigenous and enslaved people by Spanish colonizers. He is also remembered for having crisscrossed his vast diocese on foot and horseback to minister to his flock, learning Quechua and Aymara to better preach to its Indigenous…
items.t: Pope bids ‘hasta luego’ to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip

items.title: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
items.summary:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — Vast crowds of young Argentines, a generation that Catholic leaders had feared was abandoning the pews, packed the parks of Buenos Aires and cheered as if at a concert when Pope Leo XIV promised a church open to “todos, todos, todos” — everyone, everyone, everyone.

Those words, like all of Leo’s surest applause lines during the visit, belonged to his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis. So did much of the week’s adulation.

Francis’s fierce defense of the downtrodden made him a moral voice abroad but long embroiled him in political fights at home — controversy that many believe deterred him from returning as pope. More than a year after his death, the more measured Leo made the homecoming Francis never could, carrying on his legacy and helping Argentines embrace their once-polarizing pope as a unifying national figure.

“It’s as though it has finally become clear that Francis left a very important legacy, not just for Argentina but for the universal church,” said Pablo Forni, a sociologist at Argentina’s national research council, Conicet. “Leo is reaping what Francis sowed.”

Billboards welcoming Leo bore Francis’s face. Pilgrims waved signs declaring “Francisco y León, un solo corazón” — Francis and Leo, one heart. Even libertarian President Javier Milei, who once insulted Francis as “the representative of evil on earth,” declared Francis “the most important Argentine in history” at Leo’s welcome ceremony, bringing a packed hall of his political allies and foes to its feet.

A pope caught in the divide 

As archbishop of Buenos Aires, Francis —…
items.t: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them

items.title: A hidden cathedral floor emerges in Sudan, revealing one of the biggest medieval churches
items.summary:
CAIRO — Archaeologists have unearthed the original floor of a monumental medieval cathedral in northern Sudan that could be bigger than the White House, revealing the scale and architectural significance of one of Nubia’s most important Christian buildings.

A Polish-Sudanese mission earlier this month uncovered a staircase with 36-foot-high walls that led them to the original floor level of the Great Church of Jesus, probably the largest church in medieval Nubia, in Sudan’s ancient city of Old Dongola.

The church was first found in 2021, but much of it remains buried, with the staircase the only area where archaeologists managed to reach the floor.

“This was a building larger than the famous White House … and we are planning to excavate it,” said Artur Obłuski, head of the Sudanese-Polish archaeological mission.

He said it was the largest and most important church in medieval Makuria, one of three kingdoms that emerged along the middle reaches of the Nile River following the arrival of Christian missionaries in the sixth century. The church is in Old Dongola on the eastern bank of the Nile, about 100 miles southeast of modern-day Dongola. The city is known for its numerous ancient churches.

He likened the church to Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, built by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian in 537, saying that the Great Church of Jesus played a similar role in medieval Nubia and northeastern Africa through its spatial planning and construction techniques.

“In the history of architecture, certain buildings emerge that, to use a modern term, become trendsetters. Hagia Sophia in…
items.t: A hidden cathedral floor emerges in Sudan, revealing one of the biggest medieval churches

items.title: Pope in Peruvian rainforest demands justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting Amazon
items.summary:
PUCALLPA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV on Sunday demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging, illegal mining and the “insatiable thirst for domination.”

On the penultimate day of his South American odyssey, Leo traveled into the Peruvian Amazon and channeled one of Pope Francis ’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.

“The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the northeastern city of Pucallpa.

He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010-2024.

“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

Illegal mining ravaging the rainforest and driving Indigenous out 

In addition to the decades-long problem of deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Miners use makeshift suction dredges and mercury, a toxic metal, to extract gold.

Raphael Hoetmer, Western Amazon program director at Amazon Watch, said wars and conflicts around the world have driven up the price of gold, increasing demand that in turn is resulting in more…
items.t: Pope in Peruvian rainforest demands justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting Amazon

items.title: Killer drones face a reckoning as UN conference of nations considers rules on lethal AI weapons
items.summary:
GENEVA — Killer robots and drones are coming up for a reckoning this week as government envoys on Monday revved up a discussion and could decide this week whether to launch negotiations toward setting rules for use of the deadly machines — or not.

Pope Leo XIV, the U.N. chief and advocacy groups have framed the issue as an existential debate: Whether robots can be allowed to kill and whether humans must maintain some control of and accountability for use of lethal autonomous weapon systems.

Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones like Ukraine and the Middle East, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Scary would-be scenarios, like armed drones flying amok and gunning down civilians with pinpoint precision, have peppered years of discussions about killer robots. But those talks haven’t produced any international restrictions.

The United States and Russia, longtime rivals, want to limit any curbs on their ability to develop and deploy powerful new tools in the high-tech arms race — just as AI is gaining steam and changing battle plans.

Proponents of an AI weaponry rulebook say time is of the essence.

“We’re at a pivotal point now, where it’s an experimentation phase. We’re seeing some cases here, some cases there, but not full operationalization,” said Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, an advocacy group. “It will be a lot harder to regulate and create rules when these systems have already been in use for many years.”

items.t: Killer drones face a reckoning as UN conference of nations considers rules on lethal AI weapons

items.title: A home for older residents eagerly awaits Pope Leo XIV’s return to Peruvian port city
items.summary:
CALLAO, Peru — The walls of the home for older people run by Catholic religious sisters in the Peruvian port city of Callao were recently painted. The courtyard was spruced up. More importantly, its residents were filled with a renewed sense of hope. Everyone and everything is ready for the moment they have been waiting for: A visit by Pope Leo XIV.

“It’s hard to believe that he is coming to this tiny little place — a place that is small, but full of heart,” said Silvia del Castillo, 84, who has lived at the home of the Little Sisters of the Destitute Elderly for three years.

The pontiff will visit the home Monday before presiding over a Mass expected to draw more than a million people to Las Palmas Air Base in Lima.

Leo’s visit to Peru marked the final leg of his three-nation tour of South America and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that the former Robert Prevost spent there as a missionary priest and later bishop. Leo has said it was where he learned “what it means to be a shepherd.”

The pope was in Peru during the coronavirus pandemic and helped the older persons’ home at the time.

Peruvians know him as Father Roberto 

The humble home in Callao provides 60 residents with food, medicine and occasional recreational activities to keep up their spirits.

“For me, this home has meant a new life,” said Del Castillo, whose only daughter is unable to care for her due to an autoimmune disease. “When you’re old and have nowhere else to go, and people open their hearts to you, even before they open the doors of their home, you find happiness. That is…

Under a clear blue sky, thousands of pro-life demonstrators marched through the city center of The Hague on November 14. Organizers reported a record 15,000 people took part and many participants said the crowd looked noticeably larger than last year. The march began at the Malieveld, a large grassy park, a 15-minute walk away from the Dutch Parliament. items.title: The Pope has a Peruvian ID, with his Chiclayo address
items.summary:
It is not every day that a pope has a national identity card. Leo XIV does — and earlier this year, four RENIEC registrars traveled to the Vatican to update his data for a new electronic DNI 3.0, according to Peru’s state news agency Andina. He asked that his address remain registered in Chiclayo, the northern diocese where he served as bishop for nine years — a small but telling gesture from a man who has said throughout this trip that Peru is home. The DNIe 3.0 is Peru’s most secure identity document to date, launched in April 2025 and equipped with 64 security features — four times more than its predecessor. It does not expire. Robert Francis Prevost Martínez first obtained Peruvian nationality and his initial DNI in 2015, while serving as Bishop of Chiclayo. What’s even more fascinating is how Bl. Solanus was given this name to honor a Franciscan missionary in Peru. St. Francis Solanus was born in Spain in the 16th century and was received into the Franciscan Order when he was 20 years old. items.title: Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes and deep in Amazon
items.summary:
CUSCO, Peru (AP) — The plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the Amazon take center stage Sunday as Pope Leo XIV travels across Peru to visit communities high in the Andes and deep in the rainforest.

On the penultimate day of his visit to his adopted homeland, Leo is expected to echo Pope Francis, emphasizing Catholic teaching that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.

He travels first to Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, before flying to the Amazonian city of Pucallpa, where illegal mining, deforestation and threats to Indigenous communities will be central concerns.

“The church in Peru perceives the continuity of his commitment to accompany Indigenous peoples in the defense of life and the care of the territory, which is increasingly threatened by deforestation and illegal mining,” Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, president of the Amazon bishops conference, told The Associated Press.

“Leo is clearing the path laid out” by Francis on environmental protection and human rights, Barreto said. He added that the pope would hear about violence affecting children and young people.

From the Andes to the Amazon 

The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, will test the stamina of the pope, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery.

His schedule begins at the historic Sacsayhuamán fortress, where he will speak about local religious devotion. In the Plaza de Armas, he will present a shroud from the Holy See for the image of the Lord of the Earthquakes, a focus of devotion in a country prone to…

items.title: One of the secrets to a happy marriage

As I said, it’s a small thing, a simple gesture, but it isn’t really about the drink; it’s an act of kindness that unveils a hugely important reason that our marriage continues to thrive — she’s thinking of me even within the ordinary details of her life. items.title: How do we face uncertainty without allowing it to overwhelm us? This Islamic teaching shows us the way
items.summary:
For generations of Muslims, tawakkul has been an essential part of faith – making a sincere effort while recognising the limits of human control

I once asked an elderly naan seller on the streets of Kabul how he was managing to make a living. It was almost midday and he had not sold a single naan. What would he take home, I asked. “Tawakkul ba Khuda,” he replied.

He had a long silver beard, deep brown eyes and a beautiful smile. As a frontline journalist covering the Afghan war, I had heard those words many times before. From a young woman trying to establish a clothing business in the middle of the conflict, to a military commander confronting a deadly insurgency, to a school student preparing for the long and uncertain journey towards a university degree, the expression seemed to surface wherever hope and hardship met.

items.title: The reason we barely know who built the Gothic cathedrals
items.summary:
Walk into Chartres Cathedral and you are surrounded, by any measure, by one of the supreme achievements of human civilization. The light through the rose windows, the geometry of the vaulting, the carved figures on the Royal Portal, each one a minor miracle of stone. The whole building went up in roughly 26 years, after a fire destroyed the earlier structure in 1194 — an extraordinary speed for a structure of that complexity and scale. We know who ordered it built. Bishop Renaud de Mousson commissioned the reconstruction. The donors who funded the stained glass are also documented: the bakers, the fur merchants, the drapers, each guild immortalized in a panel depicting their trade alongside the saint they venerated. Their names and professions are there in the glass, permanent advertisements for piety and money. items.title: Pope’s touching prayer to the One who taught him to be a Shepherd
items.summary:
The day after his arrival in Chiclayo, the northern Peruvian diocese of which he was the bishop, Leo XIV offered a special tribute from his former cathedral on November 14, 2026. He presided over a rite of coronation of a statue of the Virgin, consecrating his ministry to her. The Cathedral of Mary of Chiclayo, a neoclassical building, begun in the 19th century and completed in the 20th, is entirely dedicated to the Virgin Mary, from its façade surmounted by a statue of “Saint Mary of the Valleys of Chiclayo,” to its four bells named Ave Maria , Assumpta , Mater Dei, and Gratia Plena. On the richly draped steps of the cathedral where he served as bishop for eight years (2015-2023), the Peruvian-American pontiff expressed his gratitude for those years, drawing applause from the crowd that filled the square. items.title: Pope’s visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
items.summary:
ZAÑA, Peru — When Susana Baca, the Latin Grammy-winning Afro-Peruvian singer, serenaded Pope Leo XIV upon his arrival in Peru, it was a sign that the visit would provide an unparalleled spotlight on the culture that grew out of the African slave trade to this country.

Baca, arguably the best-known Afro-Peruvian musician, was also Peru’s first Black Cabinet minister and became a leading figure in the campaign to end the discrimination that has long made second-class citizens of Black Peruvians and Peru’s Indigenous peoples.

The U.S.-born Leo, whose own family tree includes enslaved people and slave owners, is expected to highlight Peru’s African-descended community when he visits the hub of Afro-Peruvian culture on Saturday in the city of Zaña.

Leo will lead a prayer meeting at the sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, where he often went to pray while bishop of nearby Chiclayo.

In the 16th century, Mogrovejo was the first archbishop of Lima. He defended the rights of Indigenous and enslaved people and was known for having confirmed St. Martin de Porres, the first Black saint of the Americas and the patron saint of racial harmony, social justice and people of multiracial backgrounds.

The pope has already apologized for slavery 

In his first encyclical, “Magnificent Humanity,” Leo made a sweeping apology for the role of past popes in legitimizing slavery in the Americas and failing to condemn it for centuries. items.title: Canada: Raise your voice, bishops say
items.summary:
The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops (CCCB) is urging the nation’s Catholics and other concerned citizens to speak out about part of Bill C-41, called “the Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act.” While increasing safeguards around Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) sounds promising, the bill has two parts, one of which Canada’s bishops say is problematic.  The bill would prevent people whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness from accessing MAID, which the bishops called “a welcome step.” But the bill would also permit advance requests for euthanasia, allowing a person’s life to be ended after they have lost the capacity to understand or reconsider their earlier request. “Such requests could be acted on after the person has lost capacity, potentially years later,” according to the bishops. “These are separate issues that require separate decisions,” the CCCB said in a statement. The CCCB is asking Members of Parliament to separate the two measures, maintaining Read More…

items.title: Soccer star’s little girl steals the show
items.summary:
Turkish footballer Semih Güler might have discovered the secret to winning matches. Forget complicated tactics, extra training sessions, or a rousing halftime team talk. Apparently, all he needs is his little daughter Defne cheering him on! And he has the results to prove it. The little girl has attended two of her dad’s matches, and his team has won both. Not a bad record for such a young supporter! But forget the victories, it’s a video of the Kayserispor defender holding Defne in his arms during a post-match interview that’s really stealing our hearts. The little girl, who has Down syndrome, is clearly very much at home in her father’s world, and the affection between them is a joy to see. Speaking ahead of World Down Syndrome Day in March, Güler shared some heartfelt words about his daughter and others with the condition: “They are actually just like us. Maybe they have one extra chromosome, Read More…

items.title: Charting journal encourages body literacy for teens and adults
items.summary:
In an increasingly digital world, Natural Womanhood has gone against the tide to offer a body literacy journal women can hold in their hands. The Natural Womanhood journal guides women (and even older teens!) to learn how to chart their menstrual cycles and to pay attention to what cues their bodies are giving them. In a culture that can speak negatively about periods and women’s health in general, this journal is part of a movement to show women the truth about how we are designed and to empower them in their health and lifestyle choices. Natural Womanhood Program Manager Ryane Gibbens says this project grew out of a need for more tools that promote body literacy. Natural Womanhood, which also has an extensive online magazine, runs Cycle Mindfulness Clubs at a number of universities. items.title: Pope Leo gets rapturous welcome on return to Peru: ‘This visit is like a big party’
items.summary:
Pontiff is visiting the country, where he spent nearly a decade as bishop, during an 11-day South American tour

The walls in Chiclayo have been painted with colourful murals and banners welcoming Pope Leo XIV, but he is better known to residents of this city in northern Peru as “Padre Roberto” – a pastor who walked their streets, shared their love of local cuisine, and stood by them through natural disasters and the Covid-19 pandemic.

Robert Prevost, 71, who spent nearly a decade as the bishop here until he left in 2023, has returned to his former home as the Catholic church’s most powerful figure.

Continue reading...
